title: Many rites (CCC 1200–1206)
hookLine: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, Chaldean: one faith, many forms

lines: ORGAN HERE, ICONS AND INCENSE THERE.
cards: Two Catholic churches, one Sunday morning, a few streets apart. In the first, the priest stands at a plain altar facing the people, and an organ plays.

In the second, painted icons stretch across the front, incense hangs in the air, and nearly everything is sung, back and forth between priest and people. The prayers are different. The vestments are different.
Even the name is different: in the second church people may call it the Divine Liturgy. Yet both are Catholic, both are in communion with the Pope, and both celebrate the same Eucharist. How?

teach.h: A RITE: A WHOLE FAMILY OF WORSHIP.
teach.b: Day nine hundred forty-three met one Eastern Catholic church; today, the bigger picture. The word is rite. In ordinary speech a rite is a ceremony.
In the Catechism it means something bigger: a whole family of worship, with its own prayers, music, calendar and ways, handed down in one part of the Church.
The Catechism starts with what doesn't change: the one mystery of Christ, his death and resurrection, celebrated everywhere.

teach.h: ONE MYSTERY, TOO RICH FOR ONE FORM.
teach.b: Then a striking claim: that mystery is so rich that no single liturgical tradition can say all of it.
As the Gospel traveled, it took root among different peoples, and their worship grew in harmony with their languages and cultures. The Catechism names the traditions in use today.
The Latin, mainly the Roman rite, along with some local and religious-order rites. The Byzantine. The Alexandrian, or Coptic.
The Syriac. The Armenian. The Maronite.

Repeating the Second Vatican Council, it says the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity, and wants to keep them alive and growing. Not a main rite and some exotic extras. Equal.

But there's a limit: diversity mustn't damage unity. The rites stay one by keeping the same apostolic faith, the same sacraments, and communion with the bishops and the Pope. So the icons and the organ aren't rivals.
They're two ways of saying one thing, each fully at home in the one Church.

how: Roman-rite parishes celebrate the Mass, while Byzantine Catholic parishes celebrate what they call the Divine Liturgy; each Eastern Catholic church keeps its own liturgy, calendar and customs.

o: one single ceremony, such as a wedding Mass
a whole family of worship with its own ways
a local custom added on top of the Roman Mass

games.q: rites and what the Catechism says — tap the pairs.
p: the main part of the Latin tradition
how the Church holds the rites

s: the Eastern Catholic rites are less Catholic than the Roman rite
the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity.
the Catechism says no single tradition can say all of the mystery of Christ
the mystery is too rich for one form.
any change to a rite is fine as long as it fits the culture
diversity must not damage unity: the same faith, sacraments and communion hold the rites together.

games.q: you visit a Catholic parish of a rite you've never seen. icons, incense, everything sung. what does the Catechism say about it?
o: it's an exotic extra beside the real Mass.
it's of equal right and dignity: one faith, another form.
it's a separate church that left Rome.
games.why: repeating the Second Vatican Council, the Catechism says the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity.

practice: Let the names go by slowly, one for each breath: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, Chaldean. Notice which one you know least about, and just hold that name.
If you pray, hold up the Catholics of that rite, wherever they are.

wordCard.voice: Rite. Not one ceremony but a whole tradition of worship, with its own prayers and ways, celebrating the one mystery of Christ. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the Church's word for a rite, a received way of worship.

carryVoice: Your line: one faith, many forms. Equal right, equal dignity. Rest well.
